claims.text: Bayesian neural network formalisms distinguish between aleatoric uncertainty in likelihood models and epistemic uncertainty in parameter posteriors.
Monte Carlo Dropout during inference corresponds to variational inference with a Bernoulli variational distribution defined over network weights.
In the sparse measure experiment, the last-layer Bayesian neural network achieved a root mean square error of approximately 0.4.
Combining ensembling with variational inference approximates multimodal posterior shapes while retaining low inference computational overhead per sample.

evidence.description: The Bayesian posterior formulations isolate P(D|H) for aleatoric noise and P(H|D) for epistemic parameter uncertainty due to data limitations.
Evaluating networks with active dropout layers yields prediction samples derived from weight matrices defined as W_i = M_i * diag(z_i) with z_i following a Bernoulli distribution.
The sparse measures practical experiment using a last-layer stochastic model with hierarchical noise and graph Laplacian consistency conditions reached a prediction error RMSE of around 0.4.
In the Paperfold experiment, an ensemble of variational inference models generated marginal predictive distributions matching the exact NUTS MCMC sampler while keeping evaluation time low.

methodologies.name: Bayes-by-backprop with Reparameterization
methodologies.description: Stochastic variational inference framework that uses a deterministic reparameterization trick to enable backpropagation through variational parameters.
conditions: Gaussian variational distribution with diagonal covariance

methodologies.name: Monte Carlo Dropout (MC-Dropout)
methodologies.description: Approximate variational inference method leaving dropout active at evaluation time to obtain Monte Carlo predictions.

limitations.text: Standard MCMC algorithms require storing large parameter collections and scale poorly to high-dimensional deep neural networks.
Unimodal Gaussian variational distributions fail to capture complex multimodal posterior distributions caused by weight-space and scaling symmetries.
Monte Carlo Dropout lacks expressive power compared to full posterior sampling and may underestimate predictive uncertainty.
